newsitem.title: USA: U.S. April jobs report puts May Fed hike in limbo.
newsitem.headline: U.S. April jobs report puts May Fed hike in limbo.

text.p: A slide in the unemployment rate to its lowest level since 1973 conflicted with benign April job growth and a drop in wages and did little to clarify the future direction of U.S. interest rates, analysts said.

"It's really a mixed bag. Were it not for the drop in the unemployment rate, it would be a fairly straightforward for policymakers," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
"It's now going to be a close call," he added.

The U.S. Labor Department reported the unemployment rate dropped to 4.9 percent from 5.2 percent in March, but the key average hourly earnings component fell for the first time in six months, losing one cent to $12.14 from $12.15 in March.
Also, a 142,000 gain in April payrolls was below Wall Street expectations for a 211,000 rise and the previously reported March payroll figure was revised downward to 139,000 from 175,000.
Adding to the ambiguity of the report was the reportedly large influence of part-time workers on the drop in joblessness.
Economists said most of the change in employment as measured by the household survey was due to part-time workers, suggesting the economic impact of the unemployment drop would be muted.

"I don't think this report eliminates the possibilities (of a Fed rate hike), but you are certainly back to the scenario where probabilities have been reduced," said Kevin Flanagan, an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
The Fed raised the federal funds rate target for the first time in more than two years on March 25.
Some analysts said they will wait until the release of the May 13 retail sales report before deciding whether or not the Fed will raise rates at its next meeting on May 20.
Back in March, Fed policymakers pointed to the underlying strength in consumer spending as the main force prompting the 25-basis point rate rise.

The market struggled for direction immediately following the report's release. U.S. Treasuries jumped higher in a knee-jerk reaction, with the 30-year long bond gaining half a point, only to quickly retreat back to opening levels.
The dollar initially weakened against the mark but soon rebounded. U.S. stocks in the Dow Jones industrials index opened higher, drawing some strength from the mixed payrolls report, traders said.
"The decline in average hourly earnings should enable the (Treasury) market to hold at these levels," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
